extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of political science and comparative government; educated general readers
extracted.subtask_description: A historical and analytical account of how the U.S. Constitution and the State governments have developed in practice — covering checks and balances, growth of national power, institutional changes (President, Congress, Senate, Judiciary), and the advantages/limits of rigid constitutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Checks and balances / equilibrium of branches
rubrics_metrics.description: The Constitution was avowedly created as an instrument of checks and balances. Each branch of the National government was to restrain the others, and maintain the equipoise of the whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each branch (legislature, executive, judiciary) restrains the others; the two Houses balance one another; the National government as a whole is balanced against the State governments. Because the equilibrium is placed under a document unchangeable save by the people, no one branch has been able to absorb or override the others as can happen in parliamentary systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural struggle and expansion of political offices
rubrics_metrics.description: There is among political bodies and offices a constant strife, a struggle for existence ... and this struggle stimulates each body or office to exert its utmost force for its own preservation, and to develop its aptitudes in any direction wherein development is possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Political offices naturally tend to extend their powers and range; institutional growth often happens through competition among branches and offices rather than by deliberate design. Development in one direction may be checked by counter-pressures from other branches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive power expansion in moments of crisis
rubrics_metrics.description: The President has developed a capacity for becoming, in moments of national peril, something like a Roman dictator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In quiet times the President may be no stronger than before, but in crisis a trusted leader can cause the office to rise to great power. Historical crises can create precedents that enlarge executive authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marginalization of ministers / cabinet
rubrics_metrics.description: The ministers of the President have not become more important either singly or collectively as a cabinet. ... they have been a mere appendage to the President.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cut off from the legislature on one side and from the people on the other, ministers tend not to form a powerful collective counterweight to the President in the U.S. system as originally envisaged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Senate's increasing legislative functions and pressure on the Executive
rubrics_metrics.description: The Senate has come to press heavily on the Executive, and at the same time has developed legislative functions which, though contemplated in the Constitution, were comparatively rudimentary in the older days.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Senate has grown relatively stronger in practice than originally expected; it now exerts pressure on the Executive and performs legislative roles that were initially limited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vice-President's constitutional insignificance
rubrics_metrics.description: The Vice-President of the United States has become even more insignificant than the Constitution seemed to make him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The office holds little independent power in practice, beyond its constitutional role, and has diminished in practical importance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rise of Speaker and committee-chair oligarchy in the House
rubrics_metrics.description: The Speaker ... long held one of the leading parts in the piece, and could for many years prior to 1910 affect the course of legislation more than any other single person. An oligarchy of chairmen of the leading committees has sprung up in both Houses ... as a consequence of the increasing demands on their time as well as of the working of the committee system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concentration of power in key parliamentary roles (Speaker, committee chairs) can dominate legislative outcomes; committee system and time demands institutionalize such influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judiciary's expansion of power by interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: The Judiciary ... established its claim to powers which, though doubtless really granted, had been but faintly apprehended in 1789. ... the position which the Supreme court has taken in the scheme of government ... is greater than they foresaw.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judicial interpretation can substantially enlarge national powers and shape constitutional meaning over time; early decades saw rapid establishment of judicial authority followed by slower advance after 1830.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rigid constitutions: limits — cannot permanently restrain passions
rubrics_metrics.description: To expect any form of words ... permanently to restrain the passions and interests of men is to expect the impossible. ... Constitutions which in quiet times change gradually ... must in times of revolution be changed more boldly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rigid, written constitutions cannot by themselves prevent radical change in revolutionary times; adherence to the letter in crises can be harmful. They are not foolproof shields against popular impulses or emergencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rigid constitutions: strengths — slow change and civic formation
rubrics_metrics.description: The rigid Constitution ... opposes obstacles to rash and hasty change. It secures time for deliberation. It forces the people to think seriously before they alter it ... It forms the mind and temper of the people. It strengthens their conservative instincts ... It trains them to habits of legality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rigid constitutions make modification gradual and tentative, prevent some transient-majority demands, cultivate reverence for fundamental principles, and help inculcate civic habits necessary for stable self-government—particularly valuable where government is by public opinion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modes by which centralizing tendency has grown
rubrics_metrics.description: The centralizing tendency has shown itself and prevailed by: (1) the extensive interpretation by the judiciary of the powers which the Constitution vests in the National government; (2) the passing by Congress of statutes on topics not exclusively reserved to the States; (3) exertions of executive power which, having been approved by the people, and not condemned by the courts, have passed into precedents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These three mechanisms operate together to expand national power at the expense of state autonomy; precedents and popular approval can legitimize executive expansions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Underlying causes of centralization: economic and moral factors
rubrics_metrics.description: They are partly economical, partly moral. Steam and electricity have knit the various parts of the country closely together ... The power of the National government to stimulate or depress commerce and industries ... has given it a wide control over the material prosperity of the Union ... There has grown up a pride in the national flag, and in the National government as representing national unity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technological integration (railways, telegraph), national economic interests, population mobility, Civil War experiences, and an expanding federal bureaucracy and office-holding class all create conditions favoring centralization independent of deliberate constitutional change.

rubrics_metrics.name: State constitutions tend to imitate older models
rubrics_metrics.description: Each State makes its own Constitution; ... the people who make the constitution have lately come from other States ... in the absence of an inventive spirit ... it was the obvious course for the newer States to copy the organizations of the older States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: New states commonly replicate institutional forms, phrases, and precedents from older states (e.g., Virginia influenced Tennessee, Alabama, Mississippi, Florida), producing uniformity in outline across diverse states.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors promoting uniformity among States: migration, communication, and party system
rubrics_metrics.description: Population is in constant movement ... railway communication, newspapers, the telegraph ... political parties are the same in all the States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High mobility of people, nationwide communications, shared media, and national political parties all work over time to reduce local peculiarity and restrain the growth of purely local political systems or issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinctive regional characters of State groups
rubrics_metrics.description: The States fall naturally into five groups ... Each of these groups has something distinctive in the character of its inhabitants, which is reflected ... in the character of its government and politics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regional history, demographic composition, economic base, and settlement origins shape political character (e.g., New England Puritan influence; Southern imprint of slavery; North-West experimentalism; Pacific speculative elements), though core governmental forms remain similar.
